Religious tourism is travel undertaken for a religious purpose. The tourist goes to places of worship and holy places, and takes part in things like fairs, festivals and processions. The chapter counts religious places among the special things that make a place famous and attract tourists, and it asks us to make a list of religious sites from the map.

Cultural tourism is travel undertaken to see and understand the way of life of a region. The chapter says that through tourism the world gets introduced to a region's natural, social and cultural environment, and that the diversity of Indian culture, festivals, traditions, costumes and the variety of dishes made using Indian spices have created opportunities of tourism in India. Such a tourist goes to historical monuments, festivals and centres of art and craft.

So the difference lies in the aim and the destination: in religious tourism the aim is faith and the destination is a place of worship, while in cultural tourism the aim is to know a people's culture and the destination is a monument, a festival or a cultural centre. The chapter adds that it is necessary to preserve the cultural heritage of a country, and one place may attract both kinds of tourist.

The chapter says that visiting various places away from our homes for getting joy, entertainment, trading and staying is called tourism, so these are its first objectives. We undertake journeys for festivals, family functions, fairs, sports, wanderings and recreation, and when we reach the place we visit the exquisite and spectacular sites there. A second objective is to enjoy the special things that make a place famous, such as natural beauty, pleasant weather, exquisite scenery, hot springs, sea coasts, historical monuments, religious places and forest areas. A third objective is health, because some tourists travel to gain mental peace and physical strength through Indian Ayurveda, Yoga and Pranayam, and others come for medicinal and surgical treatment. A fourth objective is to let the world get introduced to a region's natural, social and cultural environment, and to preserve the cultural heritage of the country. Newer objectives have also appeared, such as touring without damaging the environment in ecotourism, seeing a glimpse of agricultural life in agro-tourism, and visiting the places where films are shot in film tourism.

Tourism has both good and bad effects on the environment. On the good side, the chapter says tourism is good for environmental development, because the government makes economic investment to develop natural locations, sanctuaries and national parks for the sake of the tourism industry. Housing, resorts and traffic routes are designed in an eco-friendly manner, electricity and water are used very judiciously and the concept of recycle and reuse is applied, so the natural environment is maintained and tourism develops at the same time. Considering the importance of tourism, the local residents also become aware of conserving the region's natural beauty and culture.

On the bad side, the chapter says the concept of ecotourism came into light only when it was realised that environment is degrading because of increasing population, pollution and urbanisation. Tourists themselves can degrade or damage a place, which is why ecotourism asks them to take precautions such as not throwing litter at tourist sites, avoiding noise pollution and not hurting the trees, birds and animals in the forests. So the effect of tourism on the environment depends on the care with which it is carried out.

The chapter says that restaurants, shops, transportation systems and recreational places develop because of tourism and directly contribute to the economy, while basic infrastructure improves and employment is generated, which helps the economy indirectly. Because foreign tourists also visit our places of interest, foreign currency increases in our economy, and the tourist places themselves get developed. New forms of tourism open up fresh opportunities: ecotourism, agro-tourism, for which many centres have been developed in the Pune and Kolhapur districts, film tourism at places such as the Mumbai film city and Ramoji City, and medical tourism built on cost-effective medicinal and surgical treatment. The Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation has created opportunities by providing guest houses, water sports and tourist houses near coastal areas, and a scuba-diving training centre of international standards at Tarkarli. Special tourist trains such as the Deccan Odyssey, the Palace on Wheels and the vistadome train have also become a business in themselves. Tourism further gives a social dimension by including rural lifestyle and tribal life, so that neglected components of society can be included in development. Because it earns so much without any goods being sold, tourism is called an invisible trade.

Problems: the chapter says that increasing population, pollution and urbanisation are degrading the environment, and that tourists themselves damage a place by throwing litter at tourist sites, causing noise pollution and hurting the trees, birds and animals in the forests. There are also dangers to the tourists. Accidents happen at the seaside when the timings of the high tide and the low tide are not known, or when people swim in the sea and go into deep waters. Going near sea coasts, hilltops, jungles and unknown caves without a local guide is risky, and so is clicking 'selfies' at sea-cliffs, at hill edges or with wild animals.

Measures: adopt ecotourism, so that the environment is not degraded or damaged while touring. Keep the tourist places clean and do not throw litter, avoid noise pollution and do not hurt the animals and birds. Follow the instructions written on the boards placed at the tourist places, always take a local guide, and find out the timings of the tides before going to a seaside. It is necessary to preserve the tourist places and the cultural heritage, to develop services and amenities, and to assure tourists of a safe journey. Housing, resorts and traffic routes should be designed in an eco-friendly manner, electricity and water used judiciously, and the idea of recycle and reuse applied.

The places to choose are those that have the attractions the chapter names as the reason a place becomes famous: natural beauty, pleasant weather, exquisite scenery, hot springs, sea coasts, historical monuments, religious places and forest areas. So in my district I would develop the forts and castles as historical centres, because the chapter says the forts and castles should be developed and that the buildings of famous people who have contributed in various sectors should be preserved as memorials. The forest area and the sanctuary can be developed as an ecotourism centre, since ecotourism means touring without degrading or damaging the environment. Farms near the town can be developed as agro-tourism centres, as has been done in the Pune and Kolhapur districts, where the tourist is shown a glimpse of agricultural life and lives on the farm on payment. The religious places and the fairs held there can be developed for the tourists who already come to them. For all of this, basic facilities should be developed first, tourists should be assured of a safe journey, and tourism should be encouraged through advertisements. The chapter says the hidden potential of other sites should also be developed, and if it is, local people will get employment and the district's economy will grow.

[Note: the chapter does not name any district, so the actual names of the places must be filled in by the student from his or her own district.]

Tourism is an important tertiary occupation, that is, an occupation of services, and the services a tourist needs can only be given by the people who live at that place. The chapter says that when we reach a destination we make use of the facilities provided over there and we also pay in lieu of those services or goods, so the money the tourist spends goes to local hands. Because of tourism, restaurants, shops, transportation systems and recreational places develop at the site, and each of these needs people to run it. Basic infrastructure also improves, and the chapter says employment is generated and employment opportunities become available to local people. Some work can be done only by local people, such as guiding tourists, which the chapter recommends for sea coasts, hilltops, jungles and unknown caves; in agro-tourism it is the farmers themselves who give hospitality on payment. The guest houses, water sports and tourist houses provided by the Maharashtra Tourism Development Corporation and the scuba-diving training centre at Tarkarli are further examples of local work created by tourism.

NOTICE
FOR THE ATTENTION OF ALL TOURISTS

1. Keep this tourist place clean. Do not throw litter anywhere.
2. Read and follow the instructions written on the boards placed at the tourist place.
3. Do not go near the sea coast, the hilltops, the jungle or unknown caves without a local guide.
4. Find out the timings of the high tide and the low tide before you go to the seaside.
5. Do not swim in the sea and do not go into deep waters.
6. Do not click 'selfies' at sea-cliffs, at hill edges or with wild animals.
7. Do not hurt the animals and the birds here, and do not hurt the trees.
8. Do not make loud noise. Noise pollution disturbs the birds and animals of this place.
9. Use water and electricity carefully during your stay.
10. Respect the culture of this region, and help us preserve this place for the tourists who come after you.

'Atithi Devo Bhava' means treating the guest as God, and in tourism every tourist is our guest. The chapter says that the hospitality of the Indians, along with the diversity of Indian culture, festivals, traditions, costumes and dishes, has itself resulted in opportunities of tourism in India, so hospitality is one of the reasons tourists choose to come here. A guest who is welcomed well feels safe, and the chapter says tourists should be assured of a safe journey and that all types of facilities should be developed for them. When tourists are treated well they stay longer and use more services, and since they pay for those services and goods, restaurants, shops, transport and recreational places grow, local people get employment and foreign currency increases in our economy. Agro-tourism shows this idea working directly, because there the tourist lives on the farm and accepts the hospitality of the farmers on payment. Hospitality also has a return side: just as we treat our guests as God, we should respect other countries' culture when we ourselves travel. So 'Atithi Devo Bhava' is not only a good custom but a real support to the growth of tourism, which the chapter calls an invisible trade.

| Kapeshwar | In the north-east, near Kinwat |
| Unakeshwar | In the north-east, near Kinwat, close to Kapeshwar |

Reasons for their being located here: on the map the springs are not scattered evenly. Three of them, Vajreshwari, Sav and Unhavare, lie one below the other in the narrow coastal strip of the Konkan, at the western foot of the plateau, and two more, Kapeshwar and Unakeshwar, lie side by side in the north-east. Hot springs appear where there are cracks or weak lines in the earth's crust. Water that has seeped deep into the ground is heated by the hot rock below and rises again to the surface along such cracks. The western edge of the plateau, where the Konkan meets the highland, is a line of such cracks, and that is why the Konkan springs fall almost in a line from north to south; the north and north-east springs lie along the valleys in the same way. The chapter tells us that hot springs are one of the special things that make a place famous, so these places can be developed for health tourism.

[Note: the chapter does not explain how or why hot springs are formed, and it does not name any of these places. The names have been read from the map, and the explanation of how a hot spring forms is not stated in the chapter.]

The correlation is clearest wherever the map shows a national highway and a railway running together, because tourist places are thickest along exactly those lines.

1. Mumbai - Thane - Panvel - Karjat - Khandala - Lonavala - Pune. The highway and the railway run side by side through this gap in the hills, and the Gharapuri, Karle and Bhaje caves, the hill stations of Lonavala and Khandala, and the forts of Raigad, Sinhagad and Torna all lie on or close to it. The map shows an air transport centre at both Mumbai and Pune.
2. Manmad - Chalisgaon - Verul - Khultabad - Daulatabad - Aurangabad, with Ajanta and Pitalkhora just to the north. The highway, the railway and an air transport centre at Aurangabad all meet here, and this is the thickest cluster of caves on the whole map.
3. Nashik - Igatpuri - Sangamner - Shirdi, where highway and railway again run together through a belt of tourist places.
4. Pune - Satara - Kolhapur - Sangli and Miraj, on the highways going towards Goa and Bengaluru, which carry tourists to Mahabaleshwar, Panchgani, Panhala, Ajinkyatara and Sajjangad.
5. Nagpur in the east, where several national highways radiate towards Delhi, Jabalpur, Kolkata and Hyderabad, a number of railway lines meet and there is an air transport centre; Ramtek and the caves near Pullar lie close by.

The chapter's own example fits this pattern. The Deccan Odyssey, the train started especially for tourism, originates at Mumbai and takes tourists to Nashik, Ellora, Ajanta, Kolhapur, Goa and Ratnagiri, that is, along the very corridors where the map shows highways and railways together.

The opposite is also visible on the map. Along the southern coast, at places like Harnei, Guhagar, Jaigad, Vijaydurg and Malvan, few routes reach the coast, and tourism there has not grown as it has on the Mumbai, Pune, Nashik and Aurangabad corridors. This shows that where transport routes are well developed, tourist places develop with them.
